items.title: David Torkanowsky interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019
items.q: the people who sat on the front stoop checking out the latest Sonny Stitt record

ctx.x: Oh, I’m sorry, you’re right. So I wrote this scathing response saying that you know I mean listen, after Katrina happened the then-speaker of the house Denny Hastert actually said, “New Orleans is going to be too expensive to rebuild. If people want to hear jazz they can go to Walt Disney World.” Yeah he said that. The letter I wrote him I’m surprised I didn’t get a knock on the door from the Secret Service ‘cause it was pretty caustic. But the point is no, no, no. I mean here’s the thing. New Orleans — jazz was…

why music flourished in New Orleans, why the creativity? She said, that’s easy, leisure time. In New Orleans, I mean it’s not called “The Big Easy” for nothing. And you know you could always go by so-and-so mama’s house who got some gumbo on the stove and you could make zero dollars in New Orleans and eat just fine. So people hung out, they hung out with each other and they shedded and they created, you know, music, like Ellis Marsalis, the quintet, the early quintet. They — James Black. They influenced Coltrane…

proved to be a long history of New Orleans musicians either over or under-valuing themselves he asked for way too much money. So the first jazz record contract went to five white guys from Kansas City called the Original Dixieland Jazz Band and that was the moniker for the music. We call it traditional New Orleans music. The thing about Dixieland — it sounds like circus music [scats]. For us there’s when to play two [scats] and that has to do with the second line in the streets, when to play two and when to play…
